title: Army Warns Next War Could Reach US Soil Before Deployment
excerpt: Acting chief Gen. Christopher LaNeve says power projection against China would be contested at home, as the Army rewrites its doctrine for disrupted bases, networks and supply lines.
body:
• Acting Army Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve warned at the Association of the United States Army conference in Washington that power projection against a major adversary would be contested from US soil.
  • The Army's new How the Army Fights framework trains forces to deploy, communicate and sustain operations when bases, supply lines and networks are disrupted.
  • The Pentagon's latest China report warns Beijing has placed cyber capabilities inside US critical infrastructure that could disrupt mobilisation during a conflict.
  • Confirmed drone incursions over Joint Base Langley-Eustis in Virginia and Picatinny Arsenal in New Jersey were cited as examples of the home-base threat, though not publicly attributed to China.

The US Army is preparing for a future in which its forces could be attacked at home before they deploy overseas, the service's acting chief of staff said this week, as drones, cyber operations and long-range weapons erode the assumption of a secure homeland. Gen. Christopher LaNeve made the remarks to Fox News Digital during the Association of the United States Army's annual conference in Washington, in comments also reported by Livemint.

"If we're going against a pacing threat, power projection will be contested."

— Gen. Christopher LaNeve, acting Army Chief of Staff

Why the assumption is changing

For two decades of operations in Iraq and Afghanistan, US forces could rely on secure bases, ports and supply lines at home and fight once they arrived overseas. LaNeve said that premise no longer holds against a pacing threat — the Pentagon's term for China. An adversary that can disrupt installations, transport networks and communications inside the United States could delay or degrade a deployment before it begins.

https://x.com/foxnewspolitics/status/2110777875465158723

The concern is grounded in the Pentagon's latest report on China's military capabilities, which warns that Beijing has positioned cyber capabilities inside US critical infrastructure networks that could be used to disrupt mobilisation in a conflict. Officials have also confirmed drone incursions over US installations, including Joint Base Langley-Eustis in Virginia and Picatinny Arsenal in New Jersey, without publicly attributing them to China.

The new framework: fight through disruption

The warning accompanies the rollout of How the Army Fights, the service's updated operational framework. It sets priorities for how formations train, fight and adopt new technology, with emphasis on deploying and sustaining operations while communications, supply lines and infrastructure are under attack. LaNeve described a command-and-control approach that can operate disconnected and reconnect when possible, rather than stopping when networks fail.

Installation defence is part of the same shift. LaNeve pointed to Joint Interagency Task Force 401, which works with federal and local law enforcement on counter-drone defences around bases and critical infrastructure. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said soldiers on the southern border mission are already testing counter-drone technology against real activity and carrying that experience back to their units. The Army is also adding biological incidents — disease outbreaks or deliberate attacks — to routine combat training.

Surveillance and the technology gap

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink warned on a separate panel that persistent surveillance could, within about five years or sooner, let an adversary locate forces almost anywhere based on their signature and speed. The Pentagon is responding with more survivable and autonomous systems for environments too dangerous for crewed platforms. War Secretary Pete Hegseth criticised the previous administration's pace on hypersonics, space and drones.

LaNeve closed with a limit on the technology argument: soldiers remain the service's primary platform and must keep fundamental skills for when advanced systems are unavailable. Technology, he said, is meant to make troops more capable, not replace the ability to fight without it.

What happens next

Expect the framework to flow into training rotations, base-defence budgets and exercises that simulate attacks on ports, rail and communications during mobilisation. For communities around major US bases — including the many Indian-American military families and defence workers who live near them — homeland defence is shifting from an abstract doctrine to local infrastructure, airspace monitoring and emergency planning. No specific threat or timeline was announced; the change is in planning assumptions, and in what the Army now trains for first.
